questions.q: Define a transaction and state the four ACID properties with one line each.
questions.model: A transaction is a program unit whose execution may change the database, a logical unit of work. Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: database stays consistent (e.g. A+B same before and after). Isolation: actions hidden from others until it terminates. Durability: committed updates are permanent.

questions.q: Name four problems of concurrent execution and describe each in one line.
questions.model: Lost update (W-W): one write overwrites another. Dirty read (W-R): reading an uncommitted value of a failed transaction. Incorrect summary: an aggregate mixes old and new values. Unrepeatable read (R-W): two reads of the same item return different values.

questions.q: Differentiate recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules.
questions.model: Recoverable: if Tj reads from Ti then Ti commits first. Cascadeless: reads only happen after the writer commits, so no cascading rollback. Strict: a written value cannot be read or overwritten until the writer commits or aborts. Strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable.

questions.q: State the four necessary conditions for deadlock.
questions.model: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.

questions.q: Compare deferred and immediate database modification in log-based recovery.
questions.model: Deferred: DB updated only after commit; recovery redoes committed transactions, ignores uncommitted ones (no undo). Immediate: DB updated during execution; recovery undoes uncommitted transactions using old values and redoes committed ones using new values.

questions.q: C1: Study the schedule shown. (a) List all conflicting pairs. (b) Draw the precedence graph. (c) Is it conflict serializable? Justify. (d) State what view serializability requires and name the three conditions.
questions.model: (a) R2(x)-W1(x) (T2 reads before T1 writes), R1(x)-W2(x), W1(x)-W2(x). (b) Edges 2→1 (from R2(x) before W1(x)) and 1→2 (from R1(x) before W2(x), and W1(x) before W2(x)). (c) The graph has a cycle 1⇄2, so NOT conflict serializable. (d) View serializable if view equivalent to a serial schedule: same initial reads, same update (read-from) sources, same final writes.

questions.q: C2: Transactions with timestamps T1=100, T2=200, T3=300 run the schedule shown. All RTS and WTS start at 0. (a) Trace RTS/WTS after each operation. (b) State which transaction is rolled back and why. (c) Compare timestamp ordering with two-phase locking.
questions.model: (a) R1(A): RTS(A)=100. R2(B): RTS(B)=200. W1(C): WTS(C)=100. R3(B): RTS(B)=300. R1(C): WTS(C)=100 is not greater than 100, so allowed; RTS(C)=100. W2(B): RTS(B)=300 > 200 so rollback. W3(A): RTS(A)=100 and WTS(A)=0 both ≤ 300, allowed; WTS(A)=300. (b) T2 is rolled back at W2(B) because a younger transaction (T3) already read B. (c) 2PL uses locks and can deadlock; timestamp ordering uses transaction ages, no locks and no deadlock, but conflicting transactions may be rolled back and restarted.
